documents.citation: Nash, W. J., Sellers, T. L., Talbot, S. R., Cawthorn, A. J. and Ford, W. B. (1994). The Population Biology of Abalone (Haliotis species) in Tasmania. I. Blacklip Abalone (H. rubra) from the North Coast and the Islands of Bass Strait. Sea Fisheries Division, Technical Report No. 48. ISSN 1034-3288.
documents.title: The Population Biology of Abalone (Haliotis species) in Tasmania. I. Blacklip Abalone (H. rubra) from the North Coast and the Islands of Bass Strait
documents.publisher: Sea Fisheries Division, Marine Research Laboratories - Taroona, Department of Primary Industry and Fisheries, Tasmania
documents.species: Haliotis rubra (blacklip abalone); a few H. laevigata (greenlip abalone) also collected
documents.study_area: Bass Strait, Tasmania: Hogan Islands, Kent Islands, Babel Island, Cape Barren Island, Waterhouse Island and adjacent Tasmanian coast
documents.relation_to_dataset: Original source of the UCI Abalone dataset (donated by Sam Waugh in 1995; also distributed on Kaggle and on Hugging Face as mstz/abalone).
summary: Measurements taken on every abalone (p. 8): whole weight, shucked meat weight, viscera weight, dry shell weight (dried to constant weight at 90 C), maximum shell length, minimum shell length and vertical shell height. These are the measurements of the UCI Abalone dataset.

Age = number of major growth rings + 1.5 years, following Prince et al. (1988a) (p. 9). The authors note the method has not been validated outside south-east Tasmania, and repeat analyses with 1 and 2 rings per year because studies in Victoria suggest a higher rate (McShane and Smith 1992).

Sex (male, female or immature) was determined by visual inspection of the intact gonad, with microscopic examination of uncertain cases (p. 10). Abalone were considered sexually differentiated if testis or ovary could be discerned; gonads that are only a thin veneer over the digestive gland are invariably immature (p. 11).

The Bass Strait populations are stunted. Growth is sigmoidal, so Gompertz as well as von Bertalanffy curves were fitted (Table 4). Von Bertalanffy L-infinity ranges from 121.6 to 146.1 mm (sexes combined).

Length at 50% maturity ranges from 65.3 mm (Waterhouse I.) to 82.6 mm (Hogan Is.); age at 50% maturity from 8.0 to 9.9 years (Table 5). Within a ring class, mature abalone are always larger than immature abalone (Fig. 19).
Fecundity depends on size rather than age (Figs. 21-24). Total mortality Z ranges from 0.185 to 0.265 per year with one ring per year (Table 8).
Only 33-48% of shells could be aged because of shell damage by boring organisms (Table 3).

documents.citation: Prince, J. D., Sellers, T. L., Ford, W. B. and Talbot, S. R. (1988). A method for ageing the abalone Haliotis rubra (Mollusca: Gastropoda). Australian Journal of Marine and Freshwater Research 39, 167-175.
documents.title: A Method for Ageing the Abalone Haliotis rubra (Mollusca: Gastropoda)
documents.journal: Australian Journal of Marine and Freshwater Research
documents.study_area: Blubber Head, Port Esperance, southern Tasmania (43 deg 19 min S, 147 deg 04 min E)
documents.study_period: February 1984 - October 1985 (length frequencies); tagging January 1983 - February 1985; shells for ring counts August and October 1986
documents.relation_to_dataset: Describes the ring-counting method behind the Rings column of the UCI Abalone dataset and the basis of the rule age = rings + 1.5 years.
summary: The spire of the shell is ground flat to expose a polished disc of nacre (10-15 mm), in which concentric rings are counted under a dissecting microscope (p. 170).

Three minor rings (0.02-0.05 mm thick) form at about 7.4, 11.4 and 15.7 months of age; the first major ring (0.05-0.15 mm, up to 0.3 mm) forms at about 20.6 months, and subsequent major rings at approximately annual intervals (32.7, 43.4, 59.2, 69.3, 79.8 and 89.3 months) (pp. 171-172).
Major rings form in winter (June-August), during the coldest water, not at spawning (September-November) (p. 172).
Minor rings may be lost when grinding large shells (>90 mm), so major and minor rings are counted separately (p. 171).

Growth below 80 mm is linear: A = 1.41 + 0.58 L (A in months, L in mm; r = 0.991, n = 16). Above 80 mm, von Bertalanffy with K = 0.024 per month and L-infinity = 139.7 mm, using t0 = 12.1 months (p. 171).

The interpretation appeared valid for Victorian and Tasmanian samples but may not apply in New South Wales, where no major rings were seen; the method should be validated for each stock (pp. 173-174).

documents.citation: Prince, J. D., Sellers, T. L., Ford, W. B. and Talbot, S. R. (1988). Recruitment, growth, mortality and population structure in a southern Australian population of Haliotis rubra (Mollusca: Gastropoda). Marine Biology 100, 75-82.
documents.title: Recruitment, growth, mortality and population structure in a southern Australian population of Haliotis rubra (Mollusca: Gastropoda)
documents.study_area: Blubber Head, Port Esperance, south-eastern Tasmania (43 deg 19 min S, 147 deg 04 min E)
documents.study_period: February 1984 - October 1985; breeding and emergence samples July 1986
documents.relation_to_dataset: Gives size and age at sexual maturity (relevant to the Infant category of the Sex column) and growth curves for the population in which the ageing method was validated.
summary: New recruits of 1-2 mm (30-45 days old) enter the population between October and February; a spawning season of August-January is inferred (pp. 77, 80).
Growth: L = 20.83 A - 2.46 below 80 mm (L in mm, A in years); above 80 mm, von Bertalanffy with K = 0.288 per year, L-infinity = 139.7 mm and t0 = 1.01 years (p. 78).
Natural mortality is about 0.70 per year in the second year of life (about 50% survival) and declines with age or size (Type III survivorship) (pp. 79-80).

Maturity was assessed with a gonad index (area of gonad in a cross-section of the visceral mass) and the presence of yolked eggs (p. 76). Maturity begins at about 90 mm (smallest abalone with free eggs in its gonad: 91 mm) and 4-5 years; most abalone are mature at >110 mm and 6-7 years (pp. 79, 81).
Abalone emerge from the cryptic sub-boulder habitat at about the onset of maturity; 80% of emergent abalone were larger than 90 mm (p. 79).

documents.citation: McShane, P. E. and Smith, M. G. (1992). Shell growth checks are unreliable indicators of age of the abalone Haliotis rubra (Mollusca: Gastropoda). Australian Journal of Marine and Freshwater Research 43, 1215-1219.
documents.title: Shell Growth Checks Are Unreliable Indicators of Age of the Abalone Haliotis rubra (Mollusca: Gastropoda)
documents.journal: Australian Journal of Marine and Freshwater Research
documents.study_area: Victoria, Australia: Sandpatch, Tullaburga Island and Port Fairy
documents.relation_to_dataset: Challenges the assumption of one growth ring per year that underlies age = rings + 1.5 in the UCI Abalone dataset.
summary: Tag-recapture growth was compared with growth estimated from counts of spire growth checks in three Victorian populations; the checks were not formed annually (p. 1218).
Growth estimated from growth checks differed significantly from tag-recapture growth (ANCOVA: Sandpatch F = 65.8, P < 0.001; Tullaburga Island F = 7.8, P = 0.006) (p. 1216).
Growth-check counts underestimated growth at Sandpatch and overestimated growth of large (>80 mm) abalone at Tullaburga Island (pp. 1216-1217).

Many shells could not be read because of damage by boring sponges (Cliona spp.) and polychaetes (Polydora spp.): 84 of 268 usable at Tullaburga Island, 59 of 128 at Sandpatch, none at Port Fairy (p. 1216).
Only clean shells, typically from fast-growing cryptic individuals, can be counted, which biases growth-check studies; validation is required for each population (p. 1218).
Von Bertalanffy parameters from tag recapture are given in Table 1 (p. 1217).

cross_document_notes: Disagreement on ring periodicity: Prince et al. (1988a) found approximately annual major rings in southern Tasmania; McShane and Smith (1992) found that growth checks were not annual in Victoria; Nash et al. (1994, pp. 54-55) consider McShane and Smith's general conclusion premature and report that marginal increment analysis supports one layer per year in Tasmania.
Nash et al. (1994) cite the two Prince et al. papers as 1988a (ageing method, Aust. J. Mar. Freshwater Res.) and 1988b (Marine Biology).
